description: Width tiers for Mathematics Year 3, ACARA v9. Covers all 23 descriptors across Number, Algebra, Measurement, Space, Statistics and Probability strands.
subject: Mathematics

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest engagement that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For understanding/concept descriptors: the minimum context or phenomenon that demonstrates the concept. For capability/process descriptors: the simplest task context in which the skill can be genuinely demonstrated.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intends — grounded in the most common elaboration cases. What a well-taught Y3 class would typically engage with.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new phenomena, contexts or task types. Must genuinely broaden the range of cases encountered, not increase difficulty within the same context. First Nations elaborations always appear in wider where present in ACARA source material.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA v9 elaborations are preserved verbatim as the source record for each descriptor. They ground typical_width and identify First Nations and cross-curricular directions.

AC9M3N01.minimum_width: Identify place value of digits in a five-digit number; read and write a five-digit numeral in words; place two five-digit numbers on a number line.
AC9M3N01.typical_width: Recognise, represent and order natural numbers up to at least 99 999 using place value; apply naming and writing conventions including zero as placeholder; locate on number lines; compare using < > =.
wider: Extend to six-digit numbers (hundreds of thousands), generalising the place value pattern
Compare the Hindu-Arabic place value system with other cultural counting systems — examining structural differences
Apply large number understanding to real-world data sets (populations, distances, prices) and reason about the magnitude of differences
elaborations: recognising the role of zero as a placeholder in five- and six-digit numbers
representing and ordering numbers to at least 10 000 on a number line
reading, writing and saying numbers beyond 10 000 using Australian naming conventions
comparing numbers up to and beyond 10 000 using the symbols <, > and =

AC9M3N02.minimum_width: Identify and name a unit fraction (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 or 1/10) represented by a shaded area or set model; combine two fractions with the same denominator to make a whole.
AC9M3N02.typical_width: Recognise and represent unit fractions and their multiples using area models, number lines and sets; name fractions using numerator and denominator; combine same-denominator fractions to complete the whole.
wider: Extend to fractions greater than one whole (e.g. 5/4, 7/3) as natural continuations of the multiple pattern on a number line
Connect tenths to decimal notation — showing 3/10 and 0.3 as the same position on a number line
Explore fractions in First Nations Australian sharing and distribution practices, comparing with symbolic notation
elaborations: using concrete materials or diagrams to represent unit fractions and their multiples
locating unit fractions and their multiples on a number line
combining fractions with the same denominator to make a whole, for example 3/5 + 2/5 = 1
identifying which fractions are represented when a set of objects is divided into equal groups

AC9M3N03.minimum_width: Add two three-digit numbers using place value partitioning; subtract a two-digit number from a three-digit number including at least one decomposition case.
AC9M3N03.typical_width: Add and subtract two- and three-digit numbers applying partitioning, rearranging and regrouping strategies; choose efficient strategies; record working clearly.
wider: Compare multiple strategies (partitioning, compensation, bridging) for the same problem — evaluating efficiency
Apply to financial problem contexts requiring addition and subtraction of amounts in dollars and cents
Investigate subtraction strategies from different cultural traditions and compare with standard Australian approaches
elaborations: using place value to partition numbers and add or subtract, for example 245 + 132 = 200 + 100 + 40 + 30 + 5 + 2
applying partitioning strategies to solve addition and subtraction problems, including regrouping
using number lines or empty number lines to record and communicate thinking

AC9M3N04.minimum_width: Multiply a one-digit number by a two-digit number using one named strategy; write a division number sentence connected to a known multiplication fact.
AC9M3N04.typical_width: Multiply and divide one- and two-digit numbers using number sentences, arrays and diagrams; apply and compare strategies (partitioning, doubling, repeated addition); connect multiplication and division facts.
wider: Explore the distinction between sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) division — recognising both produce the same calculation
Investigate remainders in division and what they mean in context
Apply the area model to multiplication of one-digit by two-digit numbers as a visual strategy
elaborations: representing multiplication and division problems using arrays, number lines and diagrams
using a variety of mental and written strategies to solve multiplication and division problems
connecting multiplication and division as inverse operations
using place value to multiply and divide, for example 4 × 23 = 4 × 20 + 4 × 3

AC9M3N05.minimum_width: Estimate the quantity in one collection using a stated strategy; use an estimate to check whether one calculated answer is in a reasonable range.
AC9M3N05.typical_width: Estimate quantities in collections using benchmarking, chunking and anchoring strategies; apply estimation before and after calculations to judge reasonableness; reflect on estimation accuracy.
wider: Estimate quantities in outdoor and natural contexts — number of leaves on a tree, tiles on a path — connecting to First Nations Australian knowledge of country
Investigate how rounding to different place values affects estimation accuracy — comparing nearest 10 vs nearest 100 estimates
Apply estimation to decide when approximation is sufficient vs when precision is required
elaborations: using benchmarks to estimate the number of objects in a collection, for example using 10 as a benchmark
making estimates before and after calculations to check reasonableness
identifying strategies for estimating, including chunking and using known benchmarks
discussing what makes a good estimate and how to improve accuracy

AC9M3N06.minimum_width: Translate one additive and one multiplicative word problem into number sentences; solve and write one sentence interpreting the answer in context.
AC9M3N06.typical_width: Model and solve practical additive and multiplicative problems including financial contexts; formulate as number sentences; choose calculation strategies including digital tools; interpret and communicate solutions.
wider: Solve multi-step problems requiring two or more operations, communicating the full solution process
Apply modelling to financial decision contexts — comparison shopping, calculating change, planning a budget
Investigate how mathematical modelling is used in First Nations Australian contexts such as resource sharing and planning
elaborations: using mathematical modelling to solve problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication and division in practical contexts
formulating problems using number sentences and selecting appropriate calculation strategies
using digital tools where appropriate to solve practical problems
interpreting and communicating solutions with reference to the context, including units
applying modelling to financial contexts including making purchases and giving change

AC9M3N07.minimum_width: Follow a given algorithm with three or more steps applied to two starting numbers; describe one pattern in the outputs.
AC9M3N07.typical_width: Follow and create algorithms involving sequences of steps; apply to several starting values; describe emerging patterns in number of operations and outputs.
wider: Create algorithms with decision branches ('if even/odd, then...') and trace the different pathways
Investigate a well-known number algorithm (e.g. the Collatz sequence) and describe the patterns
Express patterns generated by algorithms as generalised rules, connecting to algebraic thinking
elaborations: following a set of instructions involving a sequence of steps and decisions to investigate numbers
creating algorithms to generate number sequences and identifying patterns in the outputs
using spreadsheets or calculators to apply algorithms and explore patterns
describing and generalising patterns found in number sequences generated by algorithms

AC9M3A01.minimum_width: Write all four related facts in an addition/subtraction fact family using a part-part-whole model; find the unknown in one number sentence with the unknown in a non-standard position.
AC9M3A01.typical_width: Recognise and explain the inverse relationship using part-part-whole diagrams and bar models; partition numbers into multiple fact families; find unknowns in all positions using inverse operations.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian stories and dances that show balance and transformation, connecting to inverse operations
Connect the inverse relationship to multiplication and division — recognising the same structural pattern across operation families
Introduce unknown-in-a-sentence as a preview of algebraic equations, using box notation
elaborations: partitioning numbers using materials, part-part-whole diagrams or bar models and recording all related addition and subtraction facts
using the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to find unknown values in number sentences
exploring First Nations Australians' stories and dances that show the connection between addition and subtraction, representing this as a number sentence

AC9M3A02.minimum_width: Use one known addition fact (e.g. 6+7=13) to derive two related larger-number calculations; apply one mental strategy to solve two two-digit addition problems.
AC9M3A02.typical_width: Extend a range of addition and subtraction facts to 20 into larger-number computations; apply and choose from bridging, partitioning and compensation strategies; compute mentally without a calculator.
wider: Compare the efficiency of different mental strategies for the same computation — bridging vs compensation vs partitioning
Extend the pattern to three-digit mental computation contexts, applying the same strategy framework
Investigate how doubles and near-doubles facts provide particularly efficient mental strategy pathways
elaborations: using knowledge of addition and subtraction facts to 20 to develop mental strategies for larger numbers
partitioning using materials and part-part-whole diagrams to develop subtraction facts related to addition facts
understanding basic addition and related subtraction facts and using extensions to these facts, for example 6+6=12, 16+6=22

AC9M3A03.minimum_width: State any multiplication fact for 3, 5 or 10 and derive the two related division facts; demonstrate the 4 times table using doubling from the 2 times table.
AC9M3A03.typical_width: Recall multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10 with proficiency; explain patterns in the tables; derive and use all related division facts.
wider: Explore how the 4 times table extends via doubling to the 8 times table — generalising the doubling strategy
Apply facts to algorithmic pattern investigation — finding all multiples of 3, 4, 5 and 10 up to 100
Use multiplication facts to investigate area patterns — connecting the 3, 4, 5 times tables to rectangular arrays and area
elaborations: using concrete or virtual manipulatives, groups and repeated addition to recognise patterns and establish the 3, 4, 5 and 10 multiplication facts
recognising that when they multiply a number by 5, the resulting number will either end in 0 or 5
practising calculating and deriving multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10, explaining and recalling the patterns
systematically exploring algorithms used for repeated addition and using them to establish multiplication facts

AC9M3M01.minimum_width: Match metric units to appropriate attributes for six everyday items; use one benchmark item to estimate the measurement of two other items.
AC9M3M01.typical_width: Identify appropriate metric units across length, mass and capacity for a range of everyday items; use benchmark measurements to estimate and explain reasoning.
wider: Investigate how the metric prefix system (milli-, centi-, kilo-) applies consistently across all measurement attributes
Estimate measurements in outdoor and First Nations Australian contexts — tree heights, water vessel capacities — using culturally situated benchmarks
Examine product packaging to identify how metric units communicate quantity, and compare items at different scales
elaborations: examining the packaging on supermarket items to determine the metric unit used to describe the mass or capacity of the contents
identifying items that have a mass of one kilogram or 500 grams, or a capacity of one litre or 500 millilitres, and using these as benchmarks
estimating the height of a tree by comparing it to the height of a friend
choosing and using metres to estimate the dimensions of the classroom

AC9M3M02.minimum_width: Read three measurements from two different instruments (ruler and measuring jug); record each with its unit.
AC9M3M02.typical_width: Measure and compare objects using rulers, measuring jugs and kitchen scales; read labelled and unlabelled graduations; compare measurements across length, mass and capacity.
wider: Investigate measurement variation: measure the same object with different instruments and discuss sources of difference
Connect measurement to science investigation contexts — measuring in experiments and interpreting graduated instruments in science equipment
Explore how interpolation between graduations increases precision
elaborations: making a measuring tape using metric units and using it to measure and compare things
using centimetre grid paper to measure length and connecting with centimetre units on a ruler
measuring and comparing the mass of objects and capacity of containers using kitchen scales and measuring jugs
interpreting and explaining what the lines on a measuring jug or scales mean
comparing the capacity of different beakers used in science lessons

AC9M3M03.minimum_width: State the relationships between days, hours, minutes and seconds; convert two given time quantities between adjacent units.
AC9M3M03.typical_width: Apply formal time unit relationships across estimation and comparison contexts; estimate durations of everyday events in appropriate units; compare durations expressed in different units.
wider: Explore cultural accounts of time — how First Nations Australian seasonal calendars represent duration differently from formal clock time
Design a timetable or event sequence, applying duration estimation and addition across time units
Compare 12-hour and 24-hour time formats and investigate where each is used
elaborations: estimating how long it would take to read a set passage of text and sharing this information
planning a sequence of events based on estimates of duration, for example planning a class party
reading or setting time on digital devices to the minute or second
using sand timers and digital timers to measure and check estimates of short durations
exploring how cultural accounts of First Nations Australians include references to time and the passing of seasons

AC9M3M04.minimum_width: Read four analog clock times to the nearest minute; write each in digital notation.
AC9M3M04.typical_width: Describe the hour/minute hand relationship on analog clocks; read and record times to the nearest minute on both analog and digital clocks; set a digital device to a specified time.
wider: Convert between 12-hour and 24-hour time formats and discuss contexts where each is used (timetables, digital devices)
Apply time-to-the-minute to duration calculations — calculating elapsed time between two given times
Investigate how the clock's 60-based structure connects to ancient Babylonian mathematics
elaborations: describing the relationship between the hour and minute hands on an analog clock
reading and recording times to the nearest minute on both analog and digital clocks
setting the time on a digital device or clock
using a clock to time activities and record durations to the nearest minute

AC9M3M05.minimum_width: Classify three everyday angles as greater than, equal to, or less than a right angle; demonstrate a quarter turn physically and name it as a right angle.
AC9M3M05.typical_width: Identify angles as measures of turn; classify everyday angles relative to a right angle benchmark; compare quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns as angles in varied contexts.
wider: Program a floor robot to navigate using turns — connecting angle as a measure of turn to directional programming
Investigate right angles in construction and architecture — identifying why right angles are essential structural features
Explore how First Nations Australian dances and ceremonies use directional turns, connecting to angle measurement
elaborations: identifying angles as measures of turn in everyday situations, for example opening and closing a door, hands of a clock
comparing angles to right angles found in everyday situations, for example corners of rooms, books and rectangles
identifying angles that are less than, equal to or greater than a right angle in a range of shapes and objects
exploring how angles are used in First Nations Australian art and dance

AC9M3M06.minimum_width: Convert two money amounts between cents and dollars; show one amount using two different coin/note combinations.
AC9M3M06.typical_width: Recognise the 100-cents-per-dollar relationship; convert money amounts in both directions; represent amounts using multiple coin and note combinations; identify most efficient representations.
wider: Connect the dollar-cent relationship to decimal place value — setting up understanding of $3.75 as decimal notation
Investigate cashless payment systems and how digital transactions represent value without physical coins
Compare Australian currency structure with other countries' currencies, examining different base structures
elaborations: recognising the relationship between dollars and cents and converting between the two
representing money values using different combinations of coins and notes
solving problems involving money including making change
using digital tools to calculate with money values

AC9M3SP01.minimum_width: Identify and count faces, edges and vertices of two 3D objects; explain one geometric feature that makes each suited to its use.
AC9M3SP01.typical_width: Make, compare and classify 3D objects using geometric feature language; explain how features (shape of faces, number of edges, stability) relate to everyday purposes.
wider: Design and make a 3D object for a specific purpose, explaining feature choices — connecting to Design Technologies
Investigate geometric features in natural objects (crystals, shells, seeds) and built environments (architecture, containers)
Explore how First Nations Australians use geometric forms in tools, art and architecture
elaborations: making three-dimensional objects using a variety of materials and describing their features
identifying key features of objects and explaining why these features make them suited to their uses
comparing and classifying objects based on their features
examining how the geometric features of objects are used in everyday design

AC9M3SP02.minimum_width: Use a 2D map to locate three landmarks and describe the position of two relative to a third; create a simple map of one familiar space with four landmarks.
AC9M3SP02.typical_width: Interpret and create 2D maps of familiar environments; use directional language and spatial terms to describe positions; include a key and approximate scale.
wider: Compare drawn maps with aerial photographs — discussing what each representation emphasises
Use digital mapping tools to create and annotate maps, comparing conventions with hand-drawn versions
Explore how First Nations Australians represent country in maps, artworks and stories, contrasting with Western cartographic conventions
elaborations: interpreting and creating two-dimensional representations of familiar environments
locating key landmarks and objects relative to each other using directional language
using grid references to locate and describe positions
creating maps of familiar environments with appropriate keys and orientation indicators

AC9M3ST01.minimum_width: Identify the variable type (categorical or numerical) for a given investigation; collect data for one variable from at least 10 observations and record in a frequency table.
AC9M3ST01.typical_width: Acquire data for categorical and discrete numerical variables by observing, collecting and accessing data sets; record using frequency tables and spreadsheets; identify the variable type and explain the choice.
wider: Access an existing data set (weather records, class data) and record a relevant subset — practising secondary data acquisition
Investigate how data collection method (observation vs survey vs measurement) affects what can and cannot be found out
Explore how First Nations Australians collect and share knowledge about country and community, connecting to data collection purposes
elaborations: collecting data for categorical and discrete numerical variables to address a question of interest
recording data using frequency tables, tally marks and spreadsheets
identifying what type of variable is being investigated
accessing existing data sets and identifying variables within them

AC9M3ST02.minimum_width: Create one correctly labelled bar graph from a frequency table; identify one thing that is easier to see in one graph type compared to another.
AC9M3ST02.typical_width: Create and compare multiple graph types (picture graph, bar graph, dot plot) including using software; interpret data in terms of the question of interest; explain which representation better answers specific questions.
wider: Investigate how scale and graph type choices can make the same data look different — introducing awareness of misleading representations
Apply data interpretation to real-world decision-making: 'What would you do based on this data?'
Create graphical representations using spreadsheet software and compare with hand-drawn versions
elaborations: creating different graphical representations of data using software where appropriate
comparing the different representations and identifying and describing features of the data
interpreting the data in terms of the context of the investigation
identifying the most common and least common values in a data set from its representation

AC9M3ST03.minimum_width: With teacher guidance, complete one investigation cycle: formulate a question, collect data, create one graph, and write one sentence interpreting the result in context.
AC9M3ST03.typical_width: Conduct guided statistical investigations from question through collection, representation and interpretation; compare results with classmates; discuss what findings show in relation to the question.
wider: Conduct two investigations on similar questions with different groups and compare findings — experiencing sampling variation
Contribute data to a class investigation, combining results from multiple groups and interpreting the aggregate
Investigate a question of community relevance — e.g. school environment, local nature data — connecting statistics to purposeful inquiry
elaborations: conducting guided statistical investigations involving the collection, representation and interpretation of data
posing questions of interest and collecting data to address them
comparing findings across groups and discussing variation in results
communicating the results of statistical investigations with reference to the original question

AC9M3P01.minimum_width: Classify three everyday events as certain, impossible or a chance event; describe the most likely outcome for one chance event and explain the reasoning.
AC9M3P01.typical_width: Identify practical activities and everyday events involving chance; describe possible outcomes using likely, unlikely, certain and impossible; explain reasoning with reference to possible outcomes.
wider: Position events on an informal probability scale from impossible to certain, justifying placement
Explore equally likely outcomes (fair coin, fair spinner) and contrast with unequal likelihood contexts
Investigate how different cultures have explained uncertain events, and how probability developed as a mathematical framework
elaborations: identifying practical activities and everyday events involving chance
describing possible outcomes and events as 'likely' or 'unlikely'
identifying events as 'certain' or 'impossible' and explaining reasoning
comparing the likelihood of different outcomes in chance situations

AC9M3P02.minimum_width: List all possible outcomes for a simple experiment; conduct 20 trials and record results in a tally table; make one statement about variation between expected and actual results.
AC9M3P02.typical_width: Conduct repeated chance experiments across varied tools (coins, spinners, dice); record all outcomes; compare actual frequencies with expected outcomes; discuss variation across groups.
wider: Increase trial numbers (20 vs 50 vs 100) and compare how results change — experiencing the effect of sample size on variability
Pool results across groups and compare individual vs aggregate results — introducing the effect of larger samples
Connect chance experiments to statistical investigation (AC9M3ST03) by posing and testing a probability claim with data
elaborations: conducting repeated chance experiments such as flipping coins, spinning spinners and rolling dice
recording the results of chance experiments using tally marks and frequency tables
identifying and describing possible outcomes of chance experiments
recognising and discussing variation in results of repeated experiments
